Modern.brandNameRationale: Single word. Plane is the most basic word in architecture. A flat surface. A datum. The starting point of every drawing. We named the practice after the first move every architect makes.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern architecture practices are competing on portfolio and process. The client market has gotten more design-literate. Practices that look like product companies are winning the smaller residential and boutique commercial work.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Studio MK27 (studiomk27.com.br) sets the global modern bar. Sou Fujimoto Architects (sou-fujimoto.net) for poetic restraint. SO-IL (so-il.org) for the New York version. Locally we are competing against the design-led residential firms that publish on Instagram.
Modern.positioningStatement: A small modern practice that treats every project as one room before it is fifty.

targetAudience.primary: Homeowners, restaurateurs, and small commercial clients who already follow design accounts. They have a budget and a clear taste. They want a practice that listens before it draws.

dos: Talk about the room before the building
Show the plan, not the render
Speak to the client, not the press
donts: Photograph buildings with no people in them
Publish a manifesto on the homepage

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark only. PLANE in a precise grotesk, set with mathematical spacing. The horizontal of the A subtly extended, like a datum line crossing the wordmark. Square icon for app and social uses a single thin horizontal line.

colorPalette.name: Drafting Black
colorPalette.meaning: The color of a 6B pencil on tracing paper.

colorPalette.name: Site Yellow
colorPalette.meaning: Surveyor's flag color. The single accent.
colorPalette.usage: Section markers, key drawings, web headlines

typography.primary: GT America for the wordmark and headlines
typography.secondary: GT America Mono for dimensions and drawings
typography.rationale: One family. The mono carries the technical data on plans and elevations. The regular carries the brand.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No press releases. No glossy book monographs. No competition entries for projects we wouldn't take. No render-only marketing.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: A website that loads the floor plan first. A printed studio brochure, updated once a year. A single Instagram account with construction photos and finished plans. No reels.

Modern.tagline: An architecture office. One office. Built work.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Northpoint is the cartographic mark on a drawing — the small arrow that orients the plan. As a studio name it signals that the practice is about orientation and direction without naming a place or a partner. Stands in the lineage of single-word modern architecture studios (Office, Plot, Bjarke Ingels Group's BIG, Studio Gang) — short, slightly tradesperson-ish, no surname.
Modern.manifesto: Most architecture studio websites are about the studio. Manifesto, philosophy, team, awards, press, journal, contact. We made Northpoint because the website should be about the work. The site is a list of projects, drawn small, in chronological order. Each project opens to drawings, photographs, and a paragraph from the principal. The studio is the work.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern architecture studios have split between the design-led signature studio (BIG, MAD, Diller Scofidio + Renfro) and the commercial-led service firm (Gensler, HOK). The opening underneath is for a smaller studio with a strong drawing culture, modest visual identity, and a project-led website.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Office (officekgdvs.com) holds the single-word minimal studio slot. Studio Gang (studiogang.com) plays in the named-modern peer position. Diller Scofidio + Renfro (dsrny.com) sits in the avant-garde middle. BIG (big.dk) is the playful peer at scale. We sit alongside Office with a more drawing-led practice.
Modern.positioningStatement: Northpoint is an architecture studio whose work is mostly drawings and the buildings that come from them.
Modern.positioningRationale: We compete on drawing culture and built-work integrity. The website is a chronological list of projects. The studio is small. The partners draw.

targetAudience.primary: Developers, institutional clients, and private clients commissioning serious buildings — typically 5,000–500,000 square feet, with a multi-year programme.
behaviors: Choose studios from past built work, not from renderings.
Read drawing sets carefully.
Visit the studio before commissioning.
Sit on design-review committees.
motivations: Want a studio that draws, not just renders.
Want the principals on the project, end to end.
Want a built portfolio that holds up at 5, 10, 20 years.

dos: Lead with the drawing, then the photograph.
Write project paragraphs in the principal's voice.
Credit the project team by name on every project page.
Reference scale, programme, and site explicitly.

messagingPillars.name: Chronological list
messagingPillars.description: The site is a single chronological list of every project the studio has worked on, going backwards. Each project page is a drawing set, a built photograph, and a paragraph.

messagingPillars.name: Drawing culture
messagingPillars.description: We publish working drawings — plans, sections, axonometrics — alongside the finished photograph. The drawing is part of the project, not a marketing artifact.

messagingPillars.name: Principal on every project
messagingPillars.description: One of the two principals is the project architect on every commission, from feasibility to handover.

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark — Northpoint set in a precise grotesque, all lowercase, with a small north-arrow mark to the right. The arrow is the only logo element.

colorPalette.name: Pencil
colorPalette.meaning: Type — the colour of a dark pencil line.

colorPalette.name: Site
colorPalette.meaning: Single accent — used for the north-arrow mark.

typography.primary: A precise grotesque for the wordmark and project titles.
typography.secondary: A book serif for the project paragraphs.
typography.rationale: Two faces. The grotesque is the chrome — labels, captions, the north arrow. The serif is the writing. Drawings sit on cream paper, not white.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Two surnames, joined by an ampersand. The 19th century structure of a great American practice. The name does not reference architecture directly because at this level it does not have to. The discipline is implied by the seriousness of the name.
Luxury.story: Burnham & Wills began with two partners who had spent decades inside larger firms and wanted to take fewer commissions, more carefully. The practice has stayed small since the day it opened. The waitlist has only grown.
Luxury.industrySummary: Architecture at the top end has been chasing scale and signature. Larger offices, more projects, bigger reveals. There's a thin market in the other direction. Small practices, long timelines, projects that take five years and are designed to last a hundred.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Robert A.M. Stern (ramsa.com) holds the classical American reference. Studio Sofield (studiosofield.com) is the interiors-adjacent peer. Annabelle Selldorf (selldorf.com) is the closest in restraint and quiet ambition. We belong in their company.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small architecture practice that accepts six commissions a year and finishes each before the next begins.

targetAudience.primary: Private clients building primary or secondary residences in the $20 to $200 million range. Institutions commissioning small but meaningful buildings. People who treat the architect choice as more important than the location.

dos: Speak rarely
Use the client's surname in writing
Send paper updates by post

Luxury.logoDirection: A classical serif wordmark with elegant ligatures. A small hand-drawn ampersand becomes the firm's hallmark, used alone on stationery, the brass plaque outside the studio, and the cover of the printed brochure. The mark is small everywhere.

colorPalette.name: Drawing Ink
colorPalette.meaning: Indigo black. The color of a fountain pen on heavy paper.

colorPalette.name: Brass Hardware
colorPalette.meaning: Aged metal. The hardware on every door we specify.

typography.primary: Canela Text for the wordmark and printed material
typography.secondary: Söhne for the few digital surfaces
typography.rationale: A high contrast classical serif sets the heritage tone. A composed grotesk handles correspondence and the secure client portal. Both restrained.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No competition entries. No public press. No published monograph. No competitions for projects we wouldn't take. No client logo wall.

Luxury.tagline: A Parisian practice. Twelve commissions a year.
Luxury.brandNameRationale: Marchand is a real French surname meaning 'merchant' — an old trade name with a working-class register that has become bourgeois over generations, which is consistent with how the best European architecture practices read. Architectes (the French plural) places the brand firmly in the Continental practice tradition (Jean Nouvel, Renzo Piano Building Workshop, Atelier Jean Nouvel). The single-surname-plus-Architectes format is unmistakable.
Luxury.story: Marchand Architectes is a Paris-based practice founded by the principal in 1991. The studio takes twelve commissions a year — primarily private residences, cultural buildings, and small civic projects. The principal is involved in every project from sketch to handover.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top-of-market European architecture is dominated by a small number of signature practices with global commissions and large studios. There is a quieter market for the single-principal Continental practice — twelve commissions a year, capped roster, principal-led drawing.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Atelier Jean Nouvel (jeannouvel.com) is the signature reference. Renzo Piano Building Workshop (rpbw.com) holds the workshop-tradition peer slot. Tadao Ando Architect & Associates (tadao-ando.com) sits in the Asian-European peer position. We belong with smaller principal-led Continental practices.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A single-principal Paris practice taking twelve commissions a year across residential, cultural, and civic work.
Luxury.positioningRationale: We do not extend the studio. The principal is on every project. Commissions are accepted by referral.

targetAudience.primary: Private clients, cultural institutions, and small civic bodies commissioning significant buildings on multi-year timelines.
behaviors: Commission architecture once per generation.
Sit through design reviews in person.
Care about how the studio's other built work has aged.
Travel to see precedents.
motivations: Want a single principal, not a project director.
Want a small practice with continuity.
Want a building that will be photographed in 40 years.

dos: Address clients in formal French and English.
Sign correspondence by the principal.
Reference past commissions by year and city.
Publish a printed annual review of the studio's drawn work.
donts: No social-media presence beyond a single project archive.

messagingPillars.name: Twelve commissions
messagingPillars.description: The practice accepts twelve commissions a year. When the studio is full for the year, we say so. Commissions are accepted by referral.

messagingPillars.name: The principal draws
messagingPillars.description: Every project begins with the principal's hand drawings and ends with the principal at the handover. There is no project director layer.

messagingPillars.name: Long timelines
messagingPillars.description: Most commissions run three to seven years from first sketch to handover. The studio is happy with that timeline.

Luxury.logoDirection: A serif wordmark — Marchand Architectes set in a classical book serif with a small horizontal rule beneath the name. Letterhead register.

typography.primary: A traditional book serif for the wordmark and all printed materials.
typography.secondary: An old-style serif for body, generously set.
typography.rationale: Letterpress register. Drawing sets are presented as printed plates in linen-bound folios.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word. The most basic word for what we build. The brand is the noun. No adjective. No abstraction. We make houses, and the brand is named accordingly.
Minimal.industrySummary: Architecture practices love long, abstract names. Latin roots. Ampersands. Two-word coinages. There's an opening for one that just says what it is.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most modern practices position somewhere between art and craft. We position closer to the construction side, on purpose. The closest peers in spirit are the no-nonsense Japanese practices like Kazuyo Sejima's earliest work.
Minimal.positioningStatement: An architecture practice that builds houses. That's it.

targetAudience.primary: Homeowners who don't need their architect to also be a brand. They want a good drawing, an honest schedule, and a finished house.

dos: Show the plan
Show the schedule
Use plain English in proposals

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only. HOUSE set in a single weight grotesk, wide kerned, all caps. No icon. The proposal, the contract, and the final drawings all carry the same wordmark in the same place.

typography.rationale: One face. The drawings are the design language. The wordmark stays out of the way.

customSections.title: Not this
customSections.body: No competition entries. No monograph. No press. No published manifesto. No social media accounts beyond a single archive page.

Minimal.tagline: A drawing studio that occasionally builds.
Minimal.brandNameRationale: Plinth is the classical-architecture word for the base or pedestal a column stands on — uncommon outside the trade, immediately readable to architects. Stands in the lineage of single-word minimal architecture practices (Office, Plot, Studio) but with a more specifically architectural vocabulary, the way SO-IL, MOS, or LOT-EK use trade-specific naming.
Minimal.manifesto: Architecture studio branding has become indistinguishable from creative-agency branding — a single line of body copy, a hero render, a manifesto page. We made Plinth because the studio's actual product is drawings. The site is a black-on-cream drawing archive. The studio name appears once. No team page, no journal, no awards.
Minimal.industrySummary: Single-word minimal studio naming is well-established in architecture. There is room for a studio that takes the minimal premise into the website itself — closer to a drawing archive than a marketing surface.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Office (officekgdvs.com) is the closest peer in restraint. SO-IL (so-il.org) plays in the trade-name slot. MOS Architects (mos-office.net) holds the academic-minimal middle. LOT-EK (lot-ek.com) sits in the typographic-minimal peer position. We sit with Office and MOS, with an even smaller surface.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Plinth is an architecture studio whose website is a drawing archive and an email address.
Minimal.positioningRationale: We strip the studio surface. The website is one page of drawings, scrollable. The studio name appears once at the top.

targetAudience.primary: Clients who hire studios on the strength of drawn work.
behaviors: Read plans more carefully than press releases.
Email studios directly.
Trust the drawing.
Visit built work before commissioning.
motivations: Want a studio that publishes its drawings.
Want to skip the marketing surface.

dos: Show the drawing.
Caption with project, year, scale, programme.
Reply to emails in plain English.
Sign correspondence by the principal.

messagingPillars.name: Drawings as the site
messagingPillars.description: The website is a scrollable archive of working drawings from every project. Drawings are presented at consistent scale, with project name, year, and programme as the only caption.

messagingPillars.name: One page
messagingPillars.description: The site is one page. No subpages, no navigation, no footer.

messagingPillars.name: One email
messagingPillars.description: There is one email address. The principal reads it. Replies are plain.

Minimal.logoDirection: Plinth set in a precise grotesque, all lowercase, at small scale at the top of the page. The wordmark appears once. No emblem.

colorPalette.name: Mark
colorPalette.meaning: Single accent — used for the year markers in captions.

typography.primary: A precise grotesque for the wordmark and captions.
typography.secondary: Same family for the drawings' linework labels.
typography.rationale: One typeface across the whole site. The drawings supply the variety.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Halstead sounds like a firm that has been around. Architecture Group closes it as a B2B service category. The whole name reads like something already on a Fortune 500 facilities team's vendor list.
Corporate.industrySummary: Corporate architecture is dominated by the giant firms (HOK, Gensler, HKS, Perkins+Will). Most of them lean toward signature work. There's a quiet middle market for firms that focus on operational corporate buildings: campuses, headquarters refits, distribution centers. The buyers care about budget, schedule, and consistency more than signature.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Gensler (gensler.com) is the global giant. HOK (hok.com) holds the institutional side. Perkins+Will (perkinswill.com) is the design-leaning corporate peer. We are smaller, more responsive, and more accountable to the schedule.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Corporate architecture and program management for companies that need the building delivered on time.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Most large architecture firms over-design and under-deliver on schedule. Our pitch is the opposite. We are designed for the corporate client who has a board to answer to and a building to occupy.

targetAudience.primary: Heads of Real Estate, Corporate Facilities, and Workplace at companies of 1000 to 100000 employees. They sign multi-year contracts and they live with the consequences.

dos: Lead with schedule and budget
Show completed projects with delivery dates
Speak to the buyer

messagingPillars.name: On time, on budget
messagingPillars.description: Every project tracked against published delivery and cost milestones.

messagingPillars.name: One accountable partner
messagingPillars.description: Architecture, engineering, and program management under one contract and one principal.

messagingPillars.name: Designed for the operator
messagingPillars.description: Buildings designed for the people who run them, not the people who publish them.

Corporate.logoDirection: A wordmark with a small geometric mark to the left. The mark is a single solid right angle, suggesting structure and corner. Reads cleanly on a proposal cover, a hard hat, a name badge, and a corporate procurement deck.

colorPalette.name: Schedule Green
colorPalette.meaning: On-time accent. Used in charts and milestones.

typography.secondary: Source Serif Pro for printed RFP responses
typography.rationale: Inter scales clean across digital and printed proposals. The serif handles formal RFP submissions and printed monographs of completed work.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No residential work. No museum competitions. No press tour. No starchitect roster. The firm sells through corporate procurement, not architecture journals.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Whitlock is an English surname; Ennis is an Irish surname. The paired surnames plus the structural 'Partnership' suffix follows the long-established firm convention common in mid-tier multi-sector practices (Gensler started as M. Arthur Gensler Jr. & Associates; HOK was Hellmuth, Obata & Kassabaum). The 'Partnership' word — rather than 'Group' or 'Associates' — signals legal partnership structure and a particular American–British mid-sized firm tradition.
Corporate.manifesto: Whitlock & Ennis Partnership is an architecture and planning firm working across commercial, healthcare, civic, education, and mixed-use sectors. The firm has been in continuous operation since 1962. We have nine senior partners and a working studio of 180 staff across two offices. The buyer is an institutional client — a hospital system, a university, a municipality, a developer of substantial commercial property.
Corporate.industrySummary: Mid-tier multi-sector architecture firms face pressure from the global signature firms above and the boutique practices below. The opening is for an established mid-sized partnership with deep sector expertise across healthcare, education, civic, and commercial — and the kind of multi-year partner continuity institutional clients need.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Perkins&Will (perkinswill.com) is the multi-sector peer at scale. HOK (hok.com) holds the institutional reference. SmithGroup (smithgroup.com) sits in the multi-sector middle. HDR (hdrinc.com) plays in the engineering-architecture peer position. We sit with HDR and SmithGroup in the established multi-sector partnership category.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Whitlock & Ennis Partnership is an architecture and planning firm with nine senior partners and 180 staff working across healthcare, civic, education, and commercial sectors since 1962.
Corporate.positioningRationale: We compete on sector depth, partner continuity, and the procurement-readiness institutional clients require. The firm is structured as a working partnership, not a holding company.

targetAudience.primary: Project leads and procurement officers at hospital systems, universities, municipalities, and major commercial developers.
behaviors: Manage architect selections via formal RFP.
Maintain shortlists of three to five firms by sector.
Sit on partner-selection committees for multi-year programmes.
Renew framework agreements every three to five years.
motivations: Need a firm with documented sector experience and senior continuity.
Need a partner who can hold a programme across leadership changes on the client side.
Need a practice that is procurement-comfortable.

dos: Lead with sector expertise, project record, and partner credentials.
Speak the language of capital projects committees and procurement officers.
Publish a quarterly sector report on healthcare, education, and civic capital trends.
Reference completed projects by name, owner, and completion year.
donts: No render-heavy project page when a built photograph exists.

messagingPillars.name: Five sectors, one firm
messagingPillars.description: Active practice teams in healthcare, civic, education, commercial, and mixed-use. Each team is led by senior partners with a minimum of 20 years of sector experience.

messagingPillars.name: Partnership structure
messagingPillars.description: Nine senior partners, full equity partnership, decisions made at the partners' table. We are not a subsidiary of a larger holding company.

messagingPillars.name: Continuity across decades
messagingPillars.description: Our average partner tenure exceeds 22 years. Project teams stay together across multi-year capital programmes. Clients renew framework agreements on five-year cycles.

Corporate.logoDirection: A serif wordmark — Whitlock & Ennis Partnership set in a traditional book serif with a small horizontal rule beneath. Used in proposals, drawings, and on the partnership's office signage.

typography.primary: A traditional book serif for the wordmark and proposals.
typography.secondary: A clean enterprise grotesque for drawing sets, schedules, and reports.
typography.rationale: The serif is the firm. The grotesque is the documentation.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Draft is the architecture word for an early drawing, and the word for the air that moves through a building. Two meanings, both alive in our work. The name is loud, honest, and slightly self-deprecating: every project starts as a draft.
Creative.manifesto: Most architecture practices treat the drawing as a stage in the process. We treat it as the product. The finished building is the byproduct. We sell the drawing first, the conversation second, and the building as a consequence of both being right. We are not an architecture practice that happens to draw well. We are a drawing practice that happens to build.
Creative.industrySummary: Architecture brand is quiet and design-led. Most practices try to look like an art gallery. There's room for one that's loud, character-driven, sticker-friendly, and still serious about the work.
Creative.competitorLandscape: MOS (mos-office.net) is the closest in playful seriousness. Bureau Spectacular (bureau-spectacular.net) leans further into the cartoon end. Snarkitecture (snarkitecture.com) sells the design-installation crossover. We're sharper than any of them.
Creative.positioningStatement: An architecture practice with personality, made for clients who want a building and a conversation.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 50. Founders, restaurateurs, gallery owners, small-press publishers. People building something physical for the first time. They want an architect who is going to be fun to email.

dos: Make jokes
Annotate the drawings with margin notes
Email like a human being
donts: Quote dead architects in the homepage hero
Photograph buildings at dawn with no one in them

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark in a punchy display serif with the T crossed by a hand-drawn stroke that looks like a sketch mark. Standalone hand-drawn-T icon for stickers, social profiles, and the back of every contract.

colorPalette.name: Sketch Pink
colorPalette.meaning: Highlighter. Margin note. The annotated drawing.
colorPalette.usage: Primary brand color, hero surfaces, stickers

colorPalette.name: Blueprint Blue
colorPalette.usage: Accent, secondary type, occasional sketch backgrounds

colorPalette.name: Citrus
colorPalette.meaning: Site flag. The single warm accent.

typography.primary: Migra for the wordmark and headlines
typography.secondary: PP Neue Montreal for body and signage
typography.rationale: Migra has personality and craft. Neue Montreal keeps everything legible. The pair feels both designed and a bit hand drawn.

customSections.title: What it isn't
customSections.body: Not a starchitect. Not a quiet practice. Not afraid of color. Not too cool to annotate a margin.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: Drawings printed on real tracing paper, hand annotated, mailed to the client. Stickers on every laptop in the studio. A monthly newsletter written like a margin note. A merch line of two T-shirts and a totebag. The studio is open on Saturdays and people come by.

Creative.tagline: An office named after what it works on.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Office for Bad Buildings is a declarative naming convention borrowed from OMA's full original name (Office for Metropolitan Architecture) — a phrase that doubles as a programme. We made the practice name its own problem statement. The 'Office for X' format is among the most respected naming conventions in architecture (OMA, Office KGDVS, Office of Things). The 'Bad Buildings' designation reframes the studio's work — it specializes in the buildings nobody else wants to touch.
Creative.manifesto: Most architecture studios position themselves through the buildings they would love to design — the museum, the residence, the cultural icon. We started Office for Bad Buildings to position the studio through the buildings nobody wants to design — the strip-mall conversion, the parking deck reuse, the post-1970s office block that the city has been trying to demolish. The bad building is the work. The studio is named after it.
Creative.industrySummary: Adaptive reuse, urban infill, and brownfield conversion are growing categories with relatively few studios positioning around them. There is real space for a creative-led practice that brands itself around the difficult building rather than the iconic one.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Lacaton & Vassal (lacatonvassal.com) is the closest spiritual peer in adaptive reuse seriousness. Office KGDVS (officekgdvs.com) holds the declarative-name slot. LOT-EK (lot-ek.com) plays in the difficult-program peer position. Selldorf Architects (selldorf.com) sits in the reuse-as-art middle. We belong with Lacaton & Vassal and Office KGDVS, with a louder name and a stronger graphic identity.
Creative.positioningStatement: Office for Bad Buildings is an architecture studio that takes on adaptive reuse, brownfield conversion, and infill projects nobody else wants to design.
Creative.positioningRationale: The studio competes on the difficulty of the brief. Every project page starts with what was wrong with the building before the studio arrived. The brand is the conversion.

targetAudience.primary: Developers, municipalities, and institutional clients with a problem building they need solved.
behaviors: Inherit complicated sites.
Manage adaptive-reuse and brownfield programmes.
Care about reuse economics and embodied carbon.
Pick studios who can read a problematic building.
motivations: Want a studio that loves the difficult site.
Want a brand that does not romanticize new construction.

dos: Open every project page with what was wrong with the building.
Photograph the before condition as a first frame.
Speak in plain English about programme, budget, and constraint.
Sign the studio newsletter by the principal.
donts: No iconic-building case studies in the lead.

messagingPillars.name: Before is the first frame
messagingPillars.description: Every project page leads with the before condition — a photograph of the building as the studio inherited it, with a paragraph naming what was wrong.

messagingPillars.name: Adaptive reuse only
messagingPillars.description: We do not take new-construction commissions. Every project starts from a building that already stands.

messagingPillars.name: Embodied carbon as the metric
messagingPillars.description: Each completed project publishes its embodied-carbon savings against a hypothetical demolition-and-rebuild baseline. The numbers are the marketing.

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark — Office for Bad Buildings set in a precise grotesque, all caps, with a small horizontal rule beneath. The wordmark fits on one line at the top of every project page.

colorPalette.name: Concrete
colorPalette.meaning: Primary — the colour of a weathered concrete panel.

colorPalette.name: Caution
colorPalette.meaning: Single accent — the orange of construction tape.

typography.primary: A precise grotesque for the wordmark and project captions.
typography.secondary: A book serif for the project essays and the studio newsletter.
typography.rationale: The grotesque is the worksite. The serif is the argument.
